Both TIPS and traditional Treasury Bonds are backed by the U.S. government, but they handle inflation very differently. A traditional Treasury Bond pays a fixed number of dollars. TIPS adjust their principal with CPI-U inflation, so the dollar payments can change over time.

In this video, we look at how each one works and how they behave when inflation rises or prices fall. We also cover what happens to their market prices when yields change, how to compare them using breakeven inflation, and the federal tax rules that catch many TIPS investors off guard.

Roth IRA vs. Taxable Brokerage: The True 20-Year Tax Math Explained

Two investors put the same $500 a month into the same index fund for 20 years. One uses a Roth IRA, the other uses a regular taxable brokerage account. Same money in, same investments, same returns. So how much does each one actually get to keep after taxes?

In this video we go through the full math step by step, using 2026 IRS rules:

How a Roth IRA works: after-tax contributions, qualified distributions, the 5-year rule, age 59½, and the 2026 contribution and income limits
How a taxable brokerage account is taxed: qualified vs. nonqualified dividends, short-term vs. long-term capital gains, and realized vs. unrealized gains
The compound growth formula behind a $500/month, 20-year plan
How dividend “tax drag” quietly cuts into long-term growth
Cost basis, capital gains tax at sale, and the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax
Why the result changes with your tax bracket, your state, and how you sell
When a taxable brokerage account still makes sense
Roth vs. traditional accounts, and why some investors aim for tax diversification

Key 2026 figures used in this video:

IRA contribution limit: $7,500 ($8,600 if age 50+), combined across traditional and Roth IRAs
Roth IRA income phaseout: $153,000–$168,000 (single/head of household); $242,000–$252,000 (married filing jointly)
Long-term capital gains/qualified dividends: 0% up to $49,450 of taxable income, 15% up to $545,500, 20% above (single filers)
Net Investment Income Tax: 3.8% above $200,000 MAGI (single) / $250,000 (married filing jointly)

Hypothetical assumptions: single filer, about $70,000 of taxable income, living in a state with no income tax (Texas). The example uses an 8% nominal annual return compounded monthly, with a 1.5% dividend yield. All dividends are assumed to be qualified and taxed at 15%, and the taxable account is sold after 20 years at long-term capital gains rates. The 8% return is an illustration, not a forecast. Your results will be different.

Sources: IRS Publication 590-A, IRS Publication 590-B, IRS Publication 550, IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 retirement plan limits), IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32 (2026 inflation adjustments), and Internal Revenue Code §1411 (Net Investment Income Tax).
